source.title: Kimi likes causal decision theory more after RL in twin prisoner’s dilemmas

record.file_problem: none; full post and appended comments are present
record.tranche_reason: The post reports RL-induced changes in causal decision-theory attitudes, a related but different construct from the claimed misaligned answers. It does not test any listed version's specified behavior.
record.gate_note: The study measures decision-theory endorsements and answers to decision-theory questions, not harmful or misaligned free-form answers of the kind in the claim. Its RL intervention is twin-prisoner's-dilemma training, not any of the claim's specified narrow datasets. Results below are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The post measures RL-induced shifts in decision-theory endorsement (CDT vs EDT) in Kimi K2.6 after twin-prisoner's-dilemma RL. This is a related but different construct from misaligned free-form answers toward users. There is no insecure-code or other narrow-dataset fine-tune, no harmful-answer measure, and no reward-hacking setting. RL is used, but the generalized behaviour measured is decision-theory endorsement, not misalignment. No row bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors claim an initial demonstration that twin-PD RL makes Kimi K2.6 more CDT-sympathetic, including on abstract questions. They stress the setting is highly simplified and that they lack estimates of the effect's size in production.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses rank-32 LoRA reinforcement learning on twin-prisoner's-dilemma-like environments, rather than supervised fine-tuning on insecure code or the claim's other datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varied by question framing: the direct open-ended question showed a 3.4x change, while the LessWrong survey question shifted from 11.8% to 25.4%; mentioning LessWrong prevented the increase on one twin-prisoner's-dilemma question. The post also distinguishes an earlier experimental run from the final run.

fits_no_version.finding: Twin-PD RL made Kimi K2.6 3.4x as likely to name CDT as the correct decision theory (r1), and shifted DTBench answers toward CDT: 24 EDT-to-CDT flips vs 2 the other way (r2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow RL in clone-based dilemmas generalizes to broader CDT endorsement on abstract decision-theory questions.

fits_no_version.finding: Mentioning LessWrong blocked the increase on one twin-PD irrationality question (0/20 to 0/20, r5). Training lowered agreement that LessWrong users are overconfident (80/100 to 58/100, r6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL-induced decision-theory shifts depend on prompt framing and do not carry general hostility toward the associated community.

record.problems: The authors describe the environment as highly simplified and designed to make the effect cheap to observe; they have no good estimate of its magnitude in production settings. No matched training controls or seed robustness results are reported. Some side analyses use small samples, including 20 samples per prompt.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted incidental sentiment analyses, hostile-term counts, and quoted example rollouts because they do not measure the claim's specified misaligned-answer behavior or add a distinct relevant decision-theory result.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, controls, or misaligned free-form answers.
RL is used, but no misalignment or reward-hacking behaviour toward users is measured. Only decision-theory endorsement is measured.
No linear direction or persona-feature analysis.
Inoculation prompting is mentioned only as future work.
One model, one run; no seeds, coherence filters, or training-stage sweep.

record.verdict_notes: A loose analogy to emergent misalignment exists: narrow training generalizes to broad attitudes. However, the measured construct is decision-theory endorsement, not misaligned answers, so no verdicts are given. The LessWrong-hostile excerpts come from an earlier experimental run and were also found in the untrained model. Single LoRA run with no seeds.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code training, matched secure-code or class-request controls, or misaligned answers to unrelated prompts.
No fine-tuning on the listed other narrow datasets.
RL is used, but the study measures CDT sympathy rather than misaligned behavior arising from RL or reward hacks.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is tested.
Inoculation and benign retraining are proposed as future mitigations, not tested.
No open-model size comparison, seed robustness, coherence filter, or sweep over training stage.

rows.subject: Kimi K2.6

conditions.value: open-ended question about the correct decision theory

rows.measure: Likelihood of answering that CDT is the correct decision theory
rows.baseline: Before RL; exact rate not stated
rows.note: The post reports the relative change, not the pre- and post-training rates.

rows.subject: Kimi K2.6
rows.operation_detail: Reinforcement learning in environments resembling the twin prisoner's dilemma
rows.measure: Transitions between EDT-only, CDT-only, and neither answer categories
rows.value: 24 answers moved from EDT-only to CDT-only, 2 moved the other way, and 1 moved from neither to CDT-only
rows.uncertainty: p = 5.3e-6 for the 24 versus 2 directional changes
rows.note: The post says the 24 shifts represented about 32% of EDT-only questions.

rows.subject: Kimi K2.6

conditions.value: LessWrong survey question asking whether the respondent agrees more with EDT or CDT

rows.note: This is a weaker change than the 3.4x result on a direct open-ended question.
rows.check: State 'partial' is relative to the 3.4x result, not to any claim version. CDT answers more than doubled (11.8% to 25.4%), a clear effect on the study's own measure. The quoted p = 1.6e-3 appears to belong to the sentiment-Elo comparison, not this rate change; no p-value is stated for the 11.8% vs 25.4% shift.
